extracted.intended_audience: new or inexperienced academic researchers / students (undergraduate and beginning graduate)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for identifying, forming, and justifying a research problem/question and planning source-finding for an academic research project. Emphasizes distinguishing practical vs conceptual problems, stating significance, and locating primary/secondary/tertiary sources via library research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-step formula (Topic — Question — Significance)
rubrics_metrics.description: 1. Topic: I am studying / 2. Question: because I want to find out what/why/how, / 3. Significance: in order to help my reader understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these steps to identify the significance of your research question. Moving from step 1 to 2 marks the shift from data collector to researcher; moving from step 2 to 3 focuses on why that understanding matters. State the significance from your readers' point of view to promise them a deeper understanding in return for their interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish practical vs conceptual (research) problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical problems: 'What should we do?' — caused by a world condition that imposes tangible costs and solved by actions. Academic (conceptual) problems: 'What should we think?' — caused by lack of understanding and solved by answering questions that improve understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize whether your project is driven by a practical condition (requires doing) or by a conceptual lack of understanding (requires knowing). This distinction shapes what counts as a valid research problem and what kinds of evidence/methods are appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem structure — condition and costs/consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Both practical and conceptual problems have a two-part structure: (1) a situation or condition and (2) undesirable consequences caused by that condition (costs readers don't want to pay).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When stating a problem, describe both parts clearly. For practical problems, make the condition and tangible costs explicit. For conceptual problems, articulate the gap in understanding (condition) and the larger conceptual consequence (what else you can't know until you answer the first question).

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulate practical problems by stating condition and costs from readers' viewpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical problem example: condition — 'My brakes are screeching.' Costs — 'I might have an accident' or 'I will be late.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame practical problems from the readers' point of view so they see the cost. Anticipate the response 'So what?' and answer it by linking the condition to its costs. Continue answering 'So what?' until readers accept it as a problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulate conceptual problems by stating what you don't know
rubrics_metrics.description: A conceptual problem's condition is some version of not knowing or not understanding something. Use the three-step sentence to express the indirect question of what you don't understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrase the first gap as Q1 (a direct or indirect question). Then state the bigger, more important Q2 that cannot be answered until Q1 is answered; Q2 is the conceptual consequence that makes the research significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use chained questions (Q1 -> Q2 -> larger questions) to show increasing significance
rubrics_metrics.description: The condition and consequence of a conceptual problem are both questions: Q1 helps answer Q2; Q2 is more important than Q1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate readers asking 'So what?' and respond by showing how answering Q1 leads to insight on Q2, and possibly to even larger questions. This escalation demonstrates why the problem matters to your audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish pure vs applied research by whether the significance refers to knowing or doing
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure research: the significance (step 3) refers only to understanding. Applied research: step 3 refers to doing — practical consequences of knowing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether your project's final step is about helping readers understand (pure) or to accomplish some practical objective (applied). Example: astronomy project framed purely (understanding universe expansion) vs applied (helping astronomers correct atmospheric distortion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Test plausibility of applied significance (the a/b test)
rubrics_metrics.description: To formulate a useful applied problem, show that the answer to your conceptual question plausibly helps achieve the practical goal by asking: (a) If readers want to achieve [objective], (b) would they think they could if they knew [answer to Q1]?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this test to check whether the jump from conceptual finding to practical application is plausible (Alamo example is a stretch). If the link is weak, present the project as pure research and add the application as an extra step or in the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: State conceptual problem in the introduction; propose applications later
rubrics_metrics.description: When a conceptual question might have practical applications, formulate the problem as a purely conceptual one in the introduction and present potential practical application in the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the core research claim conceptually focused in the main presentation to avoid overstretching the significance; let the conclusion suggest how findings might be applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find problems by asking for help (talk to teachers, classmates, experts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask a variety of people (teachers, classmates, relatives, neighbors, experts) why anyone would want an answer to your question and what they would do with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use others to test whether your question is worth pursuing. If free to choose, pick a small problem that is part of a bigger one. Use teacher suggestions as starting points, but extend beyond them; don't do only what was suggested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find problems while reading: look for contradictions, inconsistencies, incomplete explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify gaps, errors, or places where sources suggest 'more questions' (often in their final pages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before claiming a source is wrong, recheck to ensure the gap is real. Many projects begin with an imaginary conversation ('Wait a minute, he's ignoring ...'). Use moves like 'Source thinks X, but I think Y' only when it shows a larger misunderstanding in the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find problems in your own drafts: examine unexpected conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: You often do your best thinking at the end of a draft; an unanticipated claim might indicate you answered a question you hadn't posed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you arrive at a surprising conclusion, ask what question it answers. Formulate that question and rework the paper to make the problem explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask whether readers will care — priority test for problems
rubrics_metrics.description: The first question about a problem should be not 'Can I solve it?' but 'Will readers think it should be solved?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If readers respond 'I don't care' your project fails. Practice framing problems to convince readers both that they should care and that the problem can be solved, especially by you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage inexperience: concrete strategies for beginners
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize uncertainty is natural. Use strategies: write regularly, break tasks into steps, get help from teachers, set realistic goals, and treat the process as a learning experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific tips include writing summaries/critiques/questions about sources, keeping a research journal, breaking tasks into manageable steps, anticipating writing/revising, asking teachers for help, and setting realistic success standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know three kinds of sources and how to use them: primary, secondary, tertiary
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary sources provide raw data (documents, texts, objects). Secondary sources are research reports using primary data for scholarly audiences. Tertiary sources synthesize secondary sources for general readers (textbooks, encyclopedias).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use primary sources as the basis for scholarly claims. Use secondary sources to situate your work and engage debates; treat a secondary as primary only when analyzing its argument. Use tertiary sources early for overview but do not rely on them as evidence in scholarly argument; follow their bibliographies to original research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer library resources and librarians over random internet searches
rubrics_metrics.description: Your library's website connects to reliable online resources; libraries provide catalogs, research guides, specialized reference works, and access to databases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If library access is limited, ask librarians about state-university resources or the Library of Congress. Use interlibrary loan when needed (start early). Talk to reference librarians (prepare specific three-step descriptions of your project) and to experts; they can help focus topics and suggest sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan your search: start with overviews, reference works, and bibliographies
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin with general or specialized encyclopedias, reference works that summarize research, and bibliographies to get an overview of the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult specialized guides to your field, annotated bibliographies, annual review journals, and book lists (e.g., Chronicle of Higher Education 'books received'). Use these to identify key journals and current research; follow references into primary literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search strategically: use library catalogs (keyword searches, browsing) rather than unguided web searching
rubrics_metrics.description: Once you have a few sources, expand your search via keyword searches and browsing within library catalogs and databases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid plunging into all sources at once. Develop a systematic plan to find data relevant to testing your hypothesis and to winnow sources to a manageable set. Use subject headings, controlled vocabularies, and browsing near key items in catalog records to discover related works.
